title: Chapter 5: Bayes’ Theorem
text:
Introduction

So we learned about conditional probabilities

We learned how the occurrence of event A affects event B (B conditional on A)

Can we figure out information on how the occurrence of event B affects event A?
We can use the conditional probability (\(\mathbb{P}(A|B)\)) to get information on the flipped conditional probability (\(\mathbb{P}(B|A)\))

title: Chapter 5: Bayes’ Theorem
text:
Bayes’ Rule for two events




Theorem: Bayes’ Rule (for two events)


For any two events \(A\) and \(B\) with nonzero probabilties,
\[\mathbb{P}(A| B) =
\frac{\mathbb{P}(A) \cdot \mathbb{P}(B|A)}
{\mathbb{P}(B)}\]

title: Chapter 5: Bayes’ Theorem
section: Calculating probability with Higher Order Multiplication Rule
text:
Calculating probability with Higher Order Multiplication Rule




Example 1


Suppose we draw 5 cards from a standard shuffled deck of 52 cards. What is the probability of a flush, that is all the cards are of the same suit (including straight flushes)?





Higher Order Multiplication Rule


\[\mathbb{P}(A_1\cap A_2 \cap  \ldots \cap A_n)=\mathbb{P}(A_1)\cdot\mathbb{P}(A_2|A_1) \cdot \\
\mathbb{P}(A_3|A_1A_2)\ldots \cdot\mathbb{P}(A_n|A_1A_2\ldots A_{n-1})\]

title: Chapter 5: Bayes’ Theorem
section: Calculating probability with Law of Total Probability
text:
Calculating probability with Law of Total Probability




Example 2


Suppose 1% of people assigned female at birth (AFAB) and 5% of people assigned male at birth (AMAB) are color-blind. Assume person born is equally likely AFAB or AMAB (not including intersex). What is the probability that a person chosen at random is color-blind?





Law of Total Probability for 2 Events


For events \(A\) and \(B\),
\[%\left(
\begin{array}{ccl}
\mathbb{P}(B)&=&\mathbb{P}(B \cap A) + \mathbb{P}(B \cap A^C)\\
           &=& \mathbb{P}(B|A) \cdot \mathbb{P}(A)+ \mathbb{P}(B | A^C)\cdot \mathbb{P}(A^C)
\end{array}
%\right)\]

text:
General Law of Total Proability


Law of Total Probability (general)


If \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^{n} = \{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n\}\) form a partition of the sample space, then for event \(B\),
\[%\left(
\begin{array}{ccl}
\mathbb{P}(B)&=& \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{P}(B \cap A_i)\\
           &=& \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{P}(B|A_i) \cdot \mathbb{P}(A_i)
\end{array}
%\right)\]

title: Chapter 5: Bayes’ Theorem
text:
Bayes’ Rule


Theorem: Bayes’ Rule


If \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\) form a partition of the sample space \(S\), with \(\mathbb{P}(A_i)>0\) for \(i=1\ldots n\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), then
\[\mathbb{P}(A_j | B) =
\frac{\mathbb{P}(B|A_j) \cdot \mathbb{P}(A_j)}
{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{P}(B|A_i) \cdot \mathbb{P}(A_i)}\]

For discrete random variables, we can use \(P(X=x)\) or \(p_X(x)\) to represent the probability that the random variable \(X\) takes on the value \(x\). And then we can discuss the probability mass function (pmf) as the probability distribution as well!
For continuous random variables, we use \(f_X(x)\) to represent the probability density function (pdf) of \(X\) at the value \(x\), BUT it is not equal to the actual probability! Aka \(f_X(x)\) does not represent a probability, but the area under the curve of \(f_X(x)\) over an interval gives us the probability.

title: Muddy Points
text:
Fall 2023

1. How do pdf, CDF, and probability interact with each other?
Let’s say we have a pdf, \(f_X(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}x^2\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 3\). This is just a function. The pdf is not used on its own to report any probability. We must integrate over the pdf to find a probability.

library("ggplot2")
eq = function(x){(1/9)*x^2}
ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1, 50)), aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun=eq) +
  xlab("x") + ylab("pdf") +
  xlim(0,3)








The total area under the pdf is 1. This makes our pdf valid.

eq = function(x){(1/9)*x^2}
ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1, 50)), aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun=eq) +
  xlab("x") + ylab("pdf") +
  xlim(0,3) +
  stat_function(fun=eq, 
                xlim = c(0, 3),
                geom = "area", 
                aes(fill = "red")) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.7, label = "AUC = 1", color = "black")








If we only look at a proportion of the area under the pdf, then we start constructing our probabilities. For example, we can look at probability that we have a value between 0 and 1.5.

ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1, 50)), aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun=eq) +
  xlab("x") + ylab("pdf") +
  xlim(0,3) +
  stat_function(fun=eq, 
                xlim = c(0, 1.5),
                geom = "area", 
                aes(fill = "blue")) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.7, label = "AUC = 0.125", color = "black")








Instead of calculating the EXACT probability for each value between 0 and 3, we can find the CDF of the pdf.
The CDF is: \[
F_X(x) = \left\{
        \begin{array}{ll}
            0 & \quad x<3 \quad \\
            \dfrac{1}{27}x^3 & \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3\quad \\
            1 & \quad x>3 \quad
        \end{array}
    \right.
\]

cdf = function(x){(1/27)*x^3}
ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1, 50)), aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun=cdf) +
  xlab("x") + ylab("CDF") +
  xlim(0,3) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








When \(x=1.5\), we can calculate the probability using the CDF. Remember that \(F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)\). So we can say \(P(X \leq 1.5) = F_X(1.5) = \dfrac{1}{27}(1.5)^3\), which equals 0.125.

cdf = function(x){(1/27)*x^3}
ggplot(data.frame(x=c(1, 50)), aes(x=x)) + 
  stat_function(fun=cdf) +
  xlab("x") + ylab("CDF") +
  xlim(0,3) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  geom_point(aes(x=1.5, y=.125), colour="blue", size=3) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.7, label = "CDF = 0.125", color = "black")

Warning in geom_point(aes(x = 1.5, y = 0.125), colour = "blue", size = 3): All aesthetics have length 1, but the data has 2 rows.
ℹ Please consider using `annotate()` or provide this layer with data containing
  a single row.









We can also calculate the probability with an integral: \(P(X \leq 1.5) = \displaystyle\int_0^{1.5} \dfrac{1}{9}x^2 dx\).
We can also find the probability that X is between two numbers. \(P(1\leq X \leq 1.5) = F_X(1.5) - F_X(1)\) or \(P(1\leq X \leq 1.5) = \displaystyle\int_1^{1.5} \dfrac{1}{9}x^2 dx\).

1. Why we are allowed to “split” the operator d/dx into two pieces as if it were a fraction when it’s an operator
Here is a pretty helpful StackExchange post talking about this!


2. How to know what to use as \(u\) and \(dv\) for integration by parts
I have two approaches to identifying \(u\) and \(dv\):

Try to find a \(u\) that will eventually differentiate into a constant. This usually works unless you’re left with a \(dv\) that is hard to integrate.

For example, \(u=x^6\). the first derivative, \(u'=6x^5\), which may lead us to do another integration by parts, but eventually, at the 6th derivative, we get 720. This means, in our integration by parts, we eventually get an integral that only has \(x\) in the function once.

In this example, \(x^6\) would result in many integration by parts. I feel like we don’t typically see that many in our work.

In Example 3.5 in Calculus Review, setting \(u=x^2\) is a bad idea because we don’t really know how to integrate \(dv=ln(x)\) into \(v\).

Try to find a \(u\) where \(du\) is the reciprocal of \(v\) or \(du\) cancels with \(v\).

title: Chapter 25: Joint densities
section: How to define the joint pdf for continuous RVs?
text:
How to define the joint pdf for continuous RVs?


For a single continuous RV \(X\) is a function \(f_X(x)\), such that for all real values \(a,b\) with \(a \leq b\), \[\mathbb{P}(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f_X(x)dx\]

For two continuous RVs (\(X\) and \(Y\)), we can define the joint pdf, \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\), such that for all real values \(a,b, c, d\) with \(a \leq b\) and \(c \leq d\), \[\mathbb{P}(a \leq X \leq b, c \leq Y \leq d) = \int_a^b \int_c^d f_{X,Y}(x,y)dydx\]

title: Chapter 25: Joint densities
section: Important properties of the joint pdf
text:
Important properties of the joint pdf

Note that \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\neq \mathbb{P}(X=x, Y=y)\)!!!
In order for \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) to be a pdf, it needs to satisfy the properties

\(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\geq 0\) for all \(x,y\)
\(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dxdy=1\)

title: Chapter 25: Joint densities
section: What is the joint cumulative distribution function?
text:
What is the joint cumulative distribution function?


Definition: Joint cumulative distribution function (Joint CDF)


The joint cumulative distribution function (cdf) of continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), is the function \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)\), such that for all real values of \(x\) and \(y\), \[F_{X,Y}(x,y)= \mathbb{P}(X \leq x, Y \leq y) = \int_{-\infty}^x\int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(s,t)dtds\]


Remarks:

The definition above for \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)\) is a function of \(x\) and \(y\).
The joint cdf at the point \((a,b)\), is \[F_{X,Y}(a,b) = \mathbb{P}(X \leq a, Y \leq b) = \int_{-\infty}^a\int_{-\infty}^b f_{X,Y}(s,t)dtds\]

title: Chapter 25: Joint densities
text:
What are the marginal pdf’s?


Definition: Marginal pdf’s


Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) are continuous r.v.’s, with joint pdf \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\). Then the marginal probability density functions are \[\begin{aligned}
f_X(x)&=& \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dy\\
f_Y(y)&=& \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dx
\end{aligned}\]

title: Chapter 25: Joint densities
section: Finding the pdf of a transformation
text:
Finding the pdf of a transformation

Let \(M\) be a transformation of \(X\) and \(Y\)
When we have a transformation of \(X\) and \(Y\), \(M\), we need to follow a specific process to find the pdf of \(M\)

We follow this process:

Start with the joint pdf for \(X\) and \(Y\)

aka \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\)

Translate the domain of \(X\) and \(Y\) to \(M\)
Find the CDF of \(M\)

aka \(F_M(m)\) or \(P(M \leq m)\)

Take the derivative of the CDF of \(M\) to find the pdf of \(M\)

aka \(f_M(m) = \dfrac{d}{dm}F_M(m)\)

The CDF is: \[
F_X(x) = \left\{

We can also calculate the probability with an integral: \(P(X \leq 1.5) = \displaystyle\int_0^{1.5} \dfrac{1}{9}x^2 dx\).
We can also find the probability that X is between two numbers. \(P(1\leq X \leq 1.5) = F_X(1.5) - F_X(1)\) or \(P(1\leq X \leq 1.5) = \displaystyle\int_1^{1.5} \dfrac{1}{9}x^2 dx\).


2. Joint vs marginal vs conditional: How are we calculating the probability?
If we start at a joint probability \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\)…. we can look at a few probabilities:

Joint probability: \(P(a \leq X \leq b, c \leq Y \leq d)\)
\[P(a \leq X \leq b, c \leq Y \leq d) = \displaystyle\int_{x=a}^{x=b}\displaystyle\int_{y=c}^{y=d} f_{X,Y}(x,y) dydx\]
Marginal probability: \(P(a \leq X \leq b)\)
\[P(a \leq X \leq b) = \displaystyle\int_{x=a}^{x=b} f_{X}(x) dx\]
OR
\[P(a \leq X \leq b) = \displaystyle\int_{x=a}^{x=b}\displaystyle\int_{y=-\inf}^{y=\inf} f_{X,Y}(x,y) dydx\]
Conditional probability: \(P(a \leq X \leq b | Y = c)\)
\[P(a \leq X \leq b | Y=c) = \displaystyle\int_{x=a}^{x=b} f_{X|Y}(x|y=c) dx\]
You cannot calculate \(P(a \leq X \leq b | Y = c)\) by \(\dfrac{P(a \leq X \leq b, Y=c)}{P(Y = c)}\) because \(P(Y = c)\) is 0. Instead, we need to find \(f_{X|Y}(x|y=c)\) by \(\dfrac{f_{X,Y}(x,y=c)}{f_{Y}(y=c)}\) and THEN integrate over X.



3. What are we actually finding by solving the double integral. In the first example, we found the probability was 1/16 after integrating but what does 1/16 mean in relation to the random variables X and Y?
It means that the volume contained by \(0\leq X \leq 1\), \(0\leq Y \leq 1/2\), and their joint pdf is 1/16 of the total volume contained by \(0\leq X \leq 2\), \(0\leq Y \leq 1\), and their joint pdf. The probability for a joint pdf is now a measure of the proportion of the volume.
This is not be confused with a probability from marginal pdf or pdf from one RV. The probability for marginal/single RV pdfs is the proportion of the area under the pdf for a specific range of values.


4. Here’s a 3D plot of one of our joint pdf’s
\[
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 5e^{-x-3y} \text{ for } 0 \leq y \leq x/2
\]

library(plotly)

x = seq(0, 5, 0.1)
y = seq(0, max(x)/2, 0.1/2)
fn = expand.grid(x=x,y=y)
fn$z = ifelse(fn$y<fn$x/2, 5*exp( (-1)*fn$x - 3*fn$y), NA)

z = matrix(fn$z, ncol = 51, nrow = 51, byrow = T)

fig <- plot_ly(x = x, y=y, z=z) %>% add_surface()

fig

title: Lesson 11: Joint distributions
text:
What is a joint distribution?




Definition: joint pmf


The joint pmf of a pair of discrete RV’s \(X\) and \(Y\) is \[\begin{aligned}
p_{X,Y}(x,y) = & \mathbb{P}(X=x \cap Y=y) \\ = & \mathbb{P}(X=x, Y=y)
\end{aligned}\]





Definition: joint pdf


The joint pdf for two continuous RVs (\(X\) and \(Y\)) is \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\), such that we have the following joint probability: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(a \leq X \leq b, & c \leq Y \leq d) = \\ & \int_a^b \int_c^d f_{X,Y}(x,y)dydx
\end{aligned}\]

title: Lesson 11: Joint distributions
text:
Important properties of joint distributions




Properties of joint pmf’s



A joint pmf \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\) must satisfy the following properties:

\(0 \geq p_{X,Y}(x,y) \leq 1\) for all \(x, y\)

 

\(\sum \limits_{\{all\ x\}} \sum \limits_{\{all\ y\}} p_{X,Y}(x,y)=1\)







Properties of joint pdf’s



A joint pdf \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) must satisfy the following properties:

\(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\geq 0\) for all \(x,y\)

 

\(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dxdy=1\)


 

Remember that \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\neq \mathbb{P}(X=x, Y=y)\)!!!

title: Lesson 11: Joint distributions
text:
Marginal distributions




Marginal pmf’s


Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) are discrete RV’s, with joint pmf \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\). Then the marginal probability mass functions are
\[p_X(x) = \sum \limits_{\{all\ y\}} p_{X,Y}(x,y)\]
\[p_Y(y) = \sum \limits_{\{all\ x\}} p_{X,Y}(x,y)\]





Marginal pdf’s


Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) are continuous RV’s, with joint pdf \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\). Then the marginal probability density functions are \[\begin{aligned}
f_X(x)&=& \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dy\\
f_Y(y)&=& \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dx
\end{aligned}\]

title: Lesson 11: Joint distributions
text:
Joint cumulative distribution functions (CDFs)




Joint CDF for discrete RVs


The joint CDF of a pair of discrete RV’s \(X\) and \(Y\) is \[\begin{aligned}
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = &\mathbb{P}(X \leq x\ and\ Y \leq y) \\ = &\mathbb{P}(X \leq x, Y \leq y)
\end{aligned}\]





Joint CDF for continuous RVs


The joint CDF of continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), is the function \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)\), such that for all real values of \(x\) and \(y\), \[\begin{aligned}
F_{X,Y}(x,y)= \mathbb{P}(X \leq x, & Y \leq y) = \\
& \int_{-\infty}^x\int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(s,t)dtds
\end{aligned}\]

Quick remarks on the joint and marginal CDF

\(F_X(x)\): right most columns of the CDF table (where the \(Y\) values are largest)
\(F_Y(y)\): bottom row of the table (where X values are largest)
\(F_X(x)=\lim\limits_{y\rightarrow\infty}F_{X, Y}(x,y)\)
\(F_Y(y)=\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}F_{X, Y}(x,y)\)

title: Lesson 11: Joint distributions
section: Recall: Finding the pdf of a transformation
text:
Recall: Finding the pdf of a transformation

Let \(M\) be a transformation of \(X\) and \(Y\): \(M = g(X, Y)\)
When we have a transformation of \(X\) and \(Y\), \(M\), we need to follow the CDF method to find the pdf of \(M\)

We follow CDF method:

Start with the joint pdf for \(X\) and \(Y\)

aka \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\)

Translate the domain of \(X\) and \(Y\) to \(M\): find possible values of \(M\)
Find the CDF of \(M\)

aka \(F_M(m) = P(M \leq m) = P(g(X, Y) \leq m)\)

Take the derivative of the CDF of \(M\) with respect to \(m\) to find the pdf of \(M\)

aka \(f_M(m) = \dfrac{d}{dm}F_M(m)\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Key concepts from Lessons 1-4:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\), \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var} + \text{Bias}^2\)
MVUE: Unbiased estimator with minimum variance
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
MLE and MME: Systematic methods for constructing estimators

. . .
Today’s Goals:

Understand sufficient statistics: data reduction without information loss
Learn the Neyman Factorization Theorem
Connect sufficiency to finding MVUEs via Rao-Blackwell
Define completeness and its role in optimal estimation




Suppose we observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from a distribution with unknown \(\theta\).
Question: Can we summarize the data with a simpler statistic \(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) without losing information about \(\theta\)?
. . .






The Key Insight



If a statistic captures all the information about \(\theta\) contained in the data, we call it sufficient for \(\theta\).


. . .
Why this matters:

Simplifies analysis and computation
Guides us to optimal estimators
Fundamental for understanding MVUEs

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Suppose we observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from a distribution with unknown \(\theta\).
Question: Can we summarize the data with a simpler statistic \(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) without losing information about \(\theta\)?
. . .






The Key Insight



If a statistic captures all the information about \(\theta\) contained in the data, we call it sufficient for \(\theta\).


. . .
Why this matters:

Simplifies analysis and computation
Guides us to optimal estimators
Fundamental for understanding MVUEs

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Mean?
Imagine you’re a consulting statistician. A colleague ran an experiment and wants your help estimating \(\theta\).
Scenario 1: They give you all raw data: \(x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 3\)
Scenario 2: They only tell you the total: \(T = x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 4\)
. . .
Question: Does Scenario 1 give you more information about \(\theta\) than Scenario 2?
. . .
If the answer is no—if knowing \(T\) tells you everything about \(\theta\)—then \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Defects (Devore 7.25)
Setup: The number of major defects on new vehicles follows \(\text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(n = 3\) vehicles with defects \(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0, X_3 = 3\).
Key Question: Would knowing only \(T = \sum X_i = 4\) provide the same information about \(\mu\) as knowing all individual \(X_i\)’s?
. . .
Consider: Given that \(T = 4\), what’s the conditional distribution of \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\)?
For the specific triple \((2, 1, 1)\):
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1)}{P(T = 4)}\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson (continued)
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^2}{2!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!}}{\frac{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4}{4!}}\]
. . .
\[= \frac{e^{-3\mu}\mu^4 / 2}{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4/24} = \frac{24}{2 \cdot 81} = \frac{4}{27}\]
. . .






Critical Observation



The \(\mu\) terms cancel out! The conditional probability doesn’t depend on \(\mu\).


This means: once we know \(T = 4\), the specific \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\) values provide no additional information about \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)



A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T = t\) does not depend on \(\theta\), for every possible value \(t\).


. . .
In other words: Once you know the value of \(T\), the distribution of the data no longer involves \(\theta\)—so no additional information about \(\theta\) can be extracted.
. . .






Intuition



\(T\) is sufficient if it “captures” all the information in the data relevant to \(\theta\). It’s sufficient to know \(T\); the raw data adds nothing more.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why is Sufficiency Important?
Practical Implications:

Data Reduction: Sufficient statistics compress data without information loss
Estimator Selection: Any good estimator should depend on the data only through sufficient statistics
Path to MVUE: Combined with other properties, leads to minimum variance estimators

. . .
Historical Note: The concept was developed by R.A. Fisher in the 1920s as part of the foundations of modern statistical inference.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Challenge
The definition of sufficiency requires computing conditional distributions—which can be quite difficult!
. . .
We need a shortcut…
. . .
Fortunately, the Neyman Factorization Theorem provides an elegant criterion based on the likelihood function.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Neyman Factorization Theorem






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)



Let \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta)\) denote the joint pmf or pdf of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\). Then \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) if and only if there exist functions \(g\) and \(h\) such that:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) depends on the data only through \(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and involves \(\theta\)
\(h\) depends on the data but not on \(\theta\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Understanding the Factorization
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \underbrace{g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta)}_{\text{Involves } \theta \text{ and data through } T} \cdot \underbrace{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}_{\text{Depends on data, not } \theta}\]
. . .
Key insight: All information about \(\theta\) is in the \(g\) factor, which depends on \(x_i\)’s only through \(T\).
. . .






Strategy for Finding Sufficient Statistics




Write down the joint pmf/pdf
Identify the part that involves \(\theta\)
Factor it so \(\theta\) appears only with a function of the data
That function is your sufficient statistic!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 1: Bernoulli Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; p) = \prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i} = p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n - \sum x_i}\]
. . .
Factorization: \[= \underbrace{p^t(1-p)^{n-t}}_{g(t; p)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).
. . .






Result



\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) (equivalently, \(\bar{X}\)) is sufficient for \(p\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 2: Poisson Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}\]
. . .
Factorization: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^t}_{g(t; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).
. . .






Result



\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 3: Exponential Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\) with pdf \(f(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x_i} = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}\]
. . .
Factorization: \[= \underbrace{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}}_{g(t; \lambda)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).
. . .






Result



\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) (equivalently, \(\bar{X}\)) is sufficient for \(\lambda\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Medical Application: Time to Disease Relapse
text:
Medical Application: Time to Disease Relapse
Cancer relapse times are often modeled with exponential distributions.

# Simulated relapse times (months) for 15 patients
set.seed(123)
true_lambda <- 0.1  # Rate parameter (relapses per month)
relapse_times <- rexp(15, rate = true_lambda)

# Sufficient statistic
T_sum <- sum(relapse_times)
T_mean <- mean(relapse_times)

cat("Individual relapse times:\n")

Individual relapse times:

cat(round(relapse_times, 2), "\n\n")

8.43 5.77 13.29 0.32 0.56 3.17 3.14 1.45 27.26 0.29 10.05 4.8 2.81 3.77 1.88 

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σx_i:", round(T_sum, 2), "months\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σx_i: 87 months

cat("Equivalently, x̄ =", round(T_mean, 2), "months\n")

Equivalently, x̄ = 5.8 months

cat("MLE of λ = 1/x̄ =", round(1/T_mean, 4), "per month")

MLE of λ = 1/x̄ = 0.1724 per month

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 4: Uniform Distribution (Devore 7.27)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta} \cdot I(0 \leq x_i \leq \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta) \cdot I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)\]
. . .
Factorization: Using indicator notation: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(t; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \max(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\).
. . .






Result



\(T = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\). Note: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient here!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Uniform Example: Visualization









Only the maximum observation matters for estimating \(\theta\)!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?
Consider two datasets with the same mean but different maxima:

# Two samples with same mean but different maxima
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)  # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10) # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 


. . .
These have the same \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)

. . .
Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses information about \(\theta\)!
The maximum captures information that the mean cannot.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Your Turn: Finding Sufficient Statistics
Exercise: Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Geometric}(p)\) with pmf \(f(x; p) = (1-p)^{x-1}p\) for \(x = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
Find a sufficient statistic for \(p\).
. . .
Solution:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; p) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1-p)^{x_i - 1}p = p^n (1-p)^{\sum x_i - n}\]
\[= \underbrace{p^n (1-p)^{t - n}}_{g(t; p)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h}\]
where \(t = \sum x_i\).
. . .
Result: \(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(p\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
When One Statistic Isn’t Enough
When there are multiple parameters, we typically need multiple sufficient statistics.
. . .






Definition: Jointly Sufficient Statistics



Statistics \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) are jointly sufficient for parameters \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T_1 = t_1, \ldots, T_k = t_k\) does not depend on any of the \(\theta_j\)’s.


. . .
Factorization Theorem (Extended): \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m) = g(t_1, \ldots, t_k; \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Normal Distribution (Both Parameters Unknown)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) unknown.
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu, \sigma^2) = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\right)^n \exp\left(-\frac{\sum(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]
. . .
Expanding \(\sum(x_i - \mu)^2 = \sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2\):
\[= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Normal Distribution (continued)
\[f = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}_{g(t_1, t_2; \mu, \sigma^2)} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}}_{h}\]
. . .






Result



\(T_1 = \sum X_i\) (or \(\bar{X}\)) and \(T_2 = \sum X_i^2\) are jointly sufficient for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\).
Equivalently, \((\bar{X}, S^2)\) are jointly sufficient.


. . .
Intuition: For normal data, the sample mean and sample variance capture all information about \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Medical Application: Blood Pressure Measurements

# Systolic blood pressure measurements (mmHg) from 30 hypertension patients
set.seed(789)
bp_data <- rnorm(30, mean = 145, sd = 15)

# Jointly sufficient statistics for (μ, σ²)
T1 <- sum(bp_data)
T2 <- sum(bp_data^2)

# Equivalent sufficient statistics
x_bar <- mean(bp_data)
s_squared <- var(bp_data)

cat("Jointly sufficient statistics:\n")

Jointly sufficient statistics:

cat("T₁ = Σxᵢ =", round(T1, 1), "\n")

T₁ = Σxᵢ = 4223.6 

cat("T₂ = Σxᵢ² =", round(T2, 1), "\n\n")

T₂ = Σxᵢ² = 597896 

cat("Equivalent form:\n")

Equivalent form:

cat("x̄ =", round(x_bar, 2), "mmHg\n")

x̄ = 140.79 mmHg

cat("S² =", round(s_squared, 2), "mmHg²")

S² = 113 mmHg²

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: The Problem: Non-Uniqueness of Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Problem: Non-Uniqueness of Sufficient Statistics
Sufficient statistics are not unique!
. . .
Trivial example: The entire dataset \((X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is always sufficient.
Less trivial: If \(T\) is sufficient, so is any one-to-one function of \(T\) (e.g., if \(\sum X_i\) is sufficient, so is \(\bar{X}\)).
. . .
Question: What is the “best” or “most efficient” sufficient statistic?
. . .






Idea



We want the sufficient statistic that achieves the greatest data reduction while still capturing all information about \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Definition: Minimal Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)



A sufficient statistic \(T\) is minimal sufficient if it is a function of every other sufficient statistic.
Equivalently: \(T\) is minimal sufficient if, for any other sufficient statistic \(T'\), we can write \(T = f(T')\) for some function \(f\).


. . .
Intuition: A minimal sufficient statistic represents the maximum possible data reduction without losing information about \(\theta\).
. . .
Example: For \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both unknown, \((\bar{X}, S^2)\) are jointly minimal sufficient—you cannot reduce the data any further without losing information.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Finding Minimal Sufficient Statistics






Practical Criterion (Devore Exercise 7.74)



\(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is minimal sufficient if for any two sample points \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)\):
\[\frac{f(\mathbf{x}; \theta)}{f(\mathbf{y}; \theta)} \text{ doesn't depend on } \theta \iff t(\mathbf{x}) = t(\mathbf{y})\]


. . .
In words: The likelihood ratio is constant in \(\theta\) if and only if the two samples have the same value of \(T\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Minimal Sufficiency for Exponential
For \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\):
\[\frac{f(\mathbf{x}; \lambda)}{f(\mathbf{y}; \lambda)} = \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}}{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum y_i}} = e^{-\lambda(\sum x_i - \sum y_i)}\]
. . .
This ratio doesn’t depend on \(\lambda\) \(\iff\) \(\sum x_i = \sum y_i\).
. . .
Therefore: \(T = \sum X_i\) is minimal sufficient for \(\lambda\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
A Cautionary Example: Cauchy Distribution
The Cauchy distribution with location parameter \(\theta\) has pdf: \[f(x; \theta) = \frac{1}{\pi[1 + (x - \theta)^2]}\]
. . .
For a random sample from Cauchy:

The ordered values \((X_{(1)}, \ldots, X_{(n)})\) are jointly sufficient
Remarkably, the ordered values are also minimal sufficient!

. . .






Surprising Result



For Cauchy, there is no reduction from the ordered sample to a simpler statistic. The full ordered data is needed to capture all information about \(\theta\).


This shows that the number of minimal sufficient statistics doesn’t always equal the number of parameters.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters for Estimation
We’ve established that sufficient statistics capture all information about \(\theta\).
Key Question: How do we use this to find better estimators?
. . .
The Rao-Blackwell Theorem provides the answer: it shows how to improve any estimator by conditioning on sufficient statistics.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Rao-Blackwell Theorem






Theorem (Rao-Blackwell)



Suppose:

\(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\)
\(U\) is any unbiased estimator for \(h(\theta)\)

Then the estimator \(U^* = E(U | T)\) satisfies:

\(U^*\) is unbiased for \(h(\theta)\)
\(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\)

with strict inequality unless \(U\) is already a function of \(T\).


. . .
In words: Conditioning an unbiased estimator on a sufficient statistic never increases variance and often decreases it.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Proof Sketch: Why Rao-Blackwell Works
Step 1: \(U^*\) is an estimator (doesn’t depend on \(\theta\))
Since \(T\) is sufficient, the conditional distribution of \(U | T\) doesn’t involve \(\theta\). Therefore \(E(U | T)\) doesn’t involve \(\theta\). ✓
. . .
Step 2: \(U^*\) is unbiased
By the Law of Total Expectation: \[E(U^*) = E[E(U | T)] = E(U) = h(\theta) \checkmark\]
. . .
Step 3: \(U^*\) has smaller variance
By the Law of Total Variance: \[\text{Var}(U) = \text{Var}(E[U|T]) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)] = \text{Var}(U^*) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)]\]
Since \(E[\text{Var}(U|T)] \geq 0\), we have \(\text{Var}(U) \geq \text{Var}(U^*)\). ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Zero-Defect Probability (Devore 7.30)
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\).
Start with a crude unbiased estimator: \[U = I(X_1 = 0) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X_1 = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } X_1 > 0 \end{cases}\]
. . .
Check: \(E(U) = P(X_1 = 0) = e^{-\mu}\) ✓ (Unbiased!)
. . .
Apply Rao-Blackwell: The sufficient statistic is \(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\).
We need: \(U^* = E(U | T) = P(X_1 = 0 | T = t)\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Poisson Example (continued)
\[P(X_1 = 0 | T = t) = \frac{P(X_1 = 0 \cap T = t)}{P(T = t)} = \frac{P(X_1 = 0) \cdot P(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i = t)}{P(T = t)}\]
. . .
Using the fact that \(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i \sim \text{Poisson}((n-1)\mu)\):
\[= \frac{e^{-\mu} \cdot \frac{e^{-(n-1)\mu}[(n-1)\mu]^t}{t!}}{\frac{e^{-n\mu}(n\mu)^t}{t!}} = \frac{(n-1)^t}{n^t} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^t\]
. . .






Improved Estimator



\[U^* = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^T\] is unbiased for \(e^{-\mu}\) with variance \(\leq\) the variance of the crude indicator!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Simulation: Comparing Estimators


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5
n <- 10
n_sims <- 5000

# Simulate Poisson samples and compute estimators
poisson_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),  # I(X_1 = 0)
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum,  # Rao-Blackwell improved
    mle = exp(-T_sum/n)  # MLE of e^(-μ)
  )

# True value
true_prob <- exp(-mu_true)

# Compare estimators
comparison <- poisson_sim |> 
  summarize(
    `E(Crude U)` = mean(crude_U),
    `E(Improved U*)` = mean(improved_U),
    `E(MLE)` = mean(mle),
    `Var(Crude U)` = var(crude_U),
    `Var(Improved U*)` = var(improved_U),
    `Var(MLE)` = var(mle)
  )

cat("True P(X = 0) = e^(-μ) =", round(true_prob, 4), "\n\n")


True P(X = 0) = e^(-μ) = 0.2231

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Key Implication: Best Estimators Use Sufficient Statistics
text:
Key Implication: Best Estimators Use Sufficient Statistics






Corollary of Rao-Blackwell



Any estimator that is not based purely on sufficient statistics is necessarily inferior to some other estimator.


. . .
Example: For Uniform\([0, \theta]\), \(\max(X_i)\) is sufficient. Any estimator using \(\bar{X}\) or \(S\) alone is suboptimal:

\(\hat{\theta}_1 = 2\bar{X}\) has variance \(\theta^2/(3n)\)
\(\hat{\theta}_2 = \frac{n+1}{n}\max(X_i)\) has variance \(\theta^2/[n(n+2)]\)

Since \(\bar{X}\) isn’t a function of \(\max(X_i)\), estimator \(\hat{\theta}_1\) loses information!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
MLEs and Sufficient Statistics






Theorem (MLEs Use Sufficient Statistics)



If \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) are jointly sufficient for \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\), then the MLEs \(\hat{\theta}_1, \ldots, \hat{\theta}_m\) can be expressed as functions of \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) alone.


. . .
Why? The likelihood factors as \(L(\theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\). Maximizing \(L\) is equivalent to maximizing \(g\), which depends on the data only through \(T\).
. . .
Practical implication: MLEs automatically “use” sufficient statistics—this is one reason they have such good properties!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Final Piece: Completeness
We’ve seen that:

Sufficient statistics capture all information about \(\theta\)
Rao-Blackwell lets us improve estimators by conditioning on sufficient statistics

. . .
Question: Given a sufficient statistic \(T\), is there a unique best unbiased estimator based on \(T\)?
. . .
The answer involves completeness—a property that ensures uniqueness.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Definition of Completeness






Definition: Complete Statistic



A statistic \(T\) is complete for \(\theta\) if for any function \(g\):
\[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]
In other words, the only function of \(T\) with expected value 0 for all \(\theta\) is the zero function (almost surely).


. . .
Intuition: Completeness means there are “no redundancies” in \(T\)—you can’t construct a non-trivial unbiased estimator of zero using \(T\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Completeness Matters






Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem



If \(T\) is a complete sufficient statistic and \(U = h(T)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(U\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).


. . .
Proof Sketch:
Suppose \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) are both unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\) and are functions of \(T\).
Then \(E[U_1 - U_2] = 0\) for all \(\theta\).
By completeness, \(U_1 - U_2 = 0\) almost surely.
Therefore \(U_1 = U_2\)—uniqueness! ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Completeness in Exponential Families






Theorem



For distributions in the exponential family (which includes Normal, Poisson, Exponential, Binomial, Gamma), the natural sufficient statistics are typically complete.


. . .
Examples of complete sufficient statistics:



Distribution
Complete Sufficient Statistic




Bernoulli\((p)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Poisson\((\mu)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Exponential\((\lambda)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\)
\((\bar{X}, S^2)\) jointly

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Normal Mean (Known Variance)
For \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) known:

\(\bar{X}\) is sufficient for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{X}\) is complete for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{X}\) is unbiased for \(\mu\)

. . .
By Lehmann-Scheffé: \(\bar{X}\) is the unique MVUE of \(\mu\).
. . .






The Power of Completeness + Sufficiency



Once we find a complete sufficient statistic, any unbiased function of it is automatically the MVUE!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Road to MVUE: Summary






Alternative path: Use Cramér-Rao bound to verify an estimator achieves minimum variance.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 1: Disease Incidence Rate
Scenario: Epidemiologists count disease cases in \(n\) geographic regions.
Let \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\) = cases in region \(i\).

# Disease cases in 8 regions
disease_cases <- c(3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 6, 3, 5)
n <- length(disease_cases)

# Sufficient statistic
T_total <- sum(disease_cases)

# MVUE of μ
mu_hat <- mean(disease_cases)

# MVUE of P(no cases) = e^(-μ)
prob_zero_hat <- (1 - 1/n)^T_total

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ =", T_total, "\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ = 35 

cat("MVUE of μ:", mu_hat, "cases per region\n")

MVUE of μ: 4.375 cases per region

cat("Improved estimate of P(no cases):", round(prob_zero_hat, 4))

Improved estimate of P(no cases): 0.0093

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 2: Drug Response Proportion
Scenario: In a clinical trial, we observe patient responses to treatment.
Let \(X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) where \(p\) = response rate.

# 50 patients: 1 = responded, 0 = no response
set.seed(111)
responses <- rbinom(50, 1, prob = 0.7)

# Sufficient statistic
T_sum <- sum(responses)

# MVUE of p (sample proportion)
p_hat <- mean(responses)

# 95% CI for p (using normal approximation)
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / length(responses))
ci <- p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ =", T_sum, "responders\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ = 40 responders

cat("MVUE of p:", p_hat, "\n")

MVUE of p: 0.8 

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci[1], 3), ",", round(ci[2], 3), ")")

95% CI: ( 0.689 , 0.911 )

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 3: Survival Time Analysis
Scenario: Patient survival times follow Exponential\((\lambda)\).

# Survival times (months) for 20 patients
survival_times <- c(14.2, 8.5, 23.1, 11.7, 19.8, 6.3, 15.4, 12.9, 
                    25.6, 9.1, 18.3, 7.8, 21.4, 13.2, 16.7, 10.5,
                    22.8, 8.9, 17.6, 11.3)

n <- length(survival_times)
T_sum <- sum(survival_times)

# MLE/MVUE of λ
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(survival_times)

# MVUE of median survival time (= log(2)/λ)
median_hat <- log(2) * mean(survival_times)

# MVUE of 1-year survival probability P(X > 12) = e^(-12λ)
surv_12 <- exp(-12 * lambda_hat)

cat("Sufficient statistic T =", round(T_sum, 1), "months\n")

Sufficient statistic T = 295.1 months

cat("MVUE of λ:", round(lambda_hat, 4), "per month\n")

MVUE of λ: 0.0678 per month

cat("Estimated median survival:", round(median_hat, 1), "months\n")

Estimated median survival: 10.2 months

cat("Estimated P(survive > 12 months):", round(surv_12, 3))

Estimated P(survive > 12 months): 0.443

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lesson 5 Summary: Key Concepts
1. Sufficiency

A statistic \(T\) is sufficient if it captures all information about \(\theta\)
Formal criterion: conditional distribution of data given \(T\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\)

. . .
2. Neyman Factorization Theorem

\(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\)
Practical tool for identifying sufficient statistics

. . .
3. Rao-Blackwell Theorem

Conditioning on sufficient statistics improves estimators
Any estimator not based on sufficient statistics is suboptimal

. . .
4. Completeness

Combined with sufficiency, guarantees unique MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Homework: Conceptual Questions

(Devore 7.38) Let \(X_i = 1\) if vehicle \(i\) passes emissions test, 0 otherwise, with \(P(X_i = 1) = p\). For \(n = 3\) vehicles, let \(T = X_1 + X_2 + X_3\). Use the definition of sufficiency to show \(T\) is sufficient for \(p\) by finding the conditional distribution of \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\) given \(T = t\).
(Devore 7.39) Components in batches of size \(k\) have proportion \(p\) satisfactory. For \(n\) batches, statistician A knows all \(X_i\)’s (satisfactory count per batch), while statistician B knows only \(T = \sum X_i\). Does A have more information about \(p\) than B?
Conceptual: Explain in your own words why the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient for \(\theta\) when sampling from Uniform\([0, \theta]\), even though it contains information about \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Homework: Finding Sufficient Statistics

(Devore 7.40) Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be lifetimes from Exponential\((\lambda)\). Use the factorization theorem to show \(\sum X_i\) is sufficient for \(\lambda\).
(Devore 7.41) For a random sample from \(f(x; \theta) = e^{-(x-\theta)}\) for \(x \geq \theta\), find a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\).
(Devore 7.43) Show that for Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both parameters unknown, \(\sum X_i\) and \(\sum X_i^2\) are jointly sufficient.
(Devore 7.70) For \(0 < \theta < 1\), consider a uniform distribution on \([\theta, 1/\theta]\). Identify a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Homework: Rao-Blackwell Applications

(Devore 7.47) For Bernoulli\((p)\) data, we want to estimate \(p(1-p)\). Start with \(U = I(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0)\) (indicator that first succeeds, second fails). Find the improved estimator \(U^* = E(U|T)\) where \(T = \sum X_i\).
(Devore 7.48) In Example 7.30, we started with \(U = I(X_1 = 0)\) to estimate \(e^{-\mu}\) for Poisson data. Now start with \(U = \frac{1}{n}\sum I(X_i = 0)\). Show that the Rao-Blackwell improved estimator is identical to the one in the example.
(Devore 7.49) For Poisson\((\mu)\), both \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\) are unbiased for \(\mu\). Consider \(\hat{\mu} = (\bar{X} + S^2)/2\). Which of \(\bar{X}\), \(S^2\), or \(\hat{\mu}\) is the best estimator? Justify using sufficiency.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Homework: Challenging Problems

(Devore 7.72) The fraction of a bottle filled follows \(f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{\theta-1}\) for \(0 < x < 1\).

Find the method of moments estimator for \(\theta\).
Is this estimator sufficient? If not, find a sufficient statistic and an estimator based on it.

(Devore 7.71) An investigator tests individuals until finding \(r\) with an allergy, where \(P(\text{allergy}) = p\). Let \(Y\) = number tested. Use the definition of sufficiency to show \(Y\) is sufficient for \(p\).
Medical Application: In a vaccine trial, adverse events follow Poisson\((\mu)\) per 1000 vaccinations. With data from \(n = 12\) groups of 1000 people:

Identify the sufficient statistic for \(\mu\)
Find the MVUE for \(\mu\)
Find an improved unbiased estimator for \(P(\text{no adverse events}) = e^{-\mu}\)

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
Use set notation, Venn diagrams, and the concepts of unions, intersections, complements, and mutually exclusive events to represent and describe events.
Apply the axioms of probability and related properties to calculate probabilities and prove simple results.

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
Set Theory (1/2)


 


Definition: Union


The union of events \(A\) and \(B\), denoted by \(A \cup B\), contains all outcomes that are in \(A\) or \(B\) or both




Definition: Intersection


The intersection of events \(A\) and \(B\), denoted by \(A \cap B\), contains all outcomes that are both in \(A\) and \(B\).



Venn diagrams

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
Set Theory (2/2)


 


Definition: Complement


The complement of event \(A\), denoted by \(A^C\) or \(A'\), contains all outcomes in the sample space \(S\) that are not in \(A\) .




Definition: Mutually Exclusive


Events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive, or disjoint, if they have no outcomes in common. In this case \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), where \(\emptyset\) is the empty set.



Venn diagrams

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
Probability Axioms




Axiom 1


For every event \(A\), \(0\leq\mathbb{P}(A)\leq 1\). Probability is between 0 and 1.




Axiom 2


For the sample space \(S\), \(\mathbb{P}(S)=1\).




Axiom 3


If \(A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots\), is a collection of disjoint events, then \[\mathbb{P}\Big( \bigcup \limits_{i=1}^{\infty}A_i\Big) =  \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(A_i).\] The probability of at least one \(A_i\) is the sum of the individual probabilities of each.

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
Some probability properties
Using the Axioms, we can prove all other probability properties! Events A, B, and C are not necessarily disjoint!




Proposition 1


For any event \(A\), \(\mathbb{P}(A)= 1 - \mathbb{P}(A^C)\)




Proposition 2


\(\mathbb{P}(\emptyset)=0\)




Proposition 3


If \(A \subseteq B\), then \(\mathbb{P}(A) \leq \mathbb{P}(B)\)





Proposition 4


\[\mathbb{P}(A \cup B) = \mathbb{P}(A) + \mathbb{P}(B) - \mathbb{P}(A \cap B)\] where \(A\) and \(B\) are not necessarily disjoint




Proposition 5


\(\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(A \cup B & \cup C) = \mathbb{P}(A) + \mathbb{P}(B) + \\ & \mathbb{P}(C) - \mathbb{P}(A \cap B) - \mathbb{P}(A \cap C) - \\ & \mathbb{P}(B \cap C) + \mathbb{P}(A \cap B \cap C) \end{aligned}\)

text:
Some final remarks on these proposition

Notice how we spliced events into multiple disjoint events

It is often easier to work with disjoint events


 

If we want to calculate the probability for one event, we may need to get creative with how we manipulate other events and the sample space

Helps us use any incomplete information we have

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
De Morgan’s Laws


Theorem: De Morgan’s 1st Law


For a collection of events (sets) \(A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots\)
\[\bigcap\limits_{i=1}^{n}A_i^C = \Big(\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{n}A_i\Big)^C\]


“all not A = \((\)at least one event A\()^C\)” or “intersection of the complements is the complement of the union”


Theorem: De Morgan’s 2nd Law


For a collection of events (sets) \(A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots\)
\[\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{n}A_i^C = \Big(\bigcap\limits_{i=1}^{n}A_i\Big)^C\]


“at least one event not A = \((\)all A\()^C\)” or “union of complements is complement of the intersection”

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
Remarks on De Morgan’s Laws

These laws also hold for infinite collections of events.
 
Draw Venn diagrams to convince yourself that these are true!
 
These laws are very useful when calculating probabilities.

This is because calculating the probability of the intersection of events is often much easier than the union of events.
This is not obvious right now, but we will see in the coming chapters why.

title: Lesson 3: Language of Probability
text:
Partitions




Definition: Partition


A set of events \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\) create a partition of \(A\), if

the \(A_i\)’s are disjoint (mutually exclusive) and
\(\bigcup \limits_{i=1}^n A_i = A\)





Example 2



If \(A \subset B\), then \(\{A, B \cap A^C\}\) is a partition of \(B\).
If \(S = \bigcup \limits_{i=1}^n A_i\), and the \(A_i\)’s are disjoint, then the \(A_i\)’s are a partition of the sample space.







Creating partitions is sometimes used to help calculate probabilities, since by Axiom 3 we can add the probabilities of disjoint events.

title: Lesson 12: Independence and Conditioning
section: How do we represent conditional pmfs/pdfs?
text:
How do we represent conditional pmfs/pdfs?
For events:
\[P(A | B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\]




For discrete RVs:


\[p_{X|Y}(x|y) = P(X=x|Y=y) = \dfrac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}\] \[p_{Y|X}(y|x) = P(Y=y|X=x) = \dfrac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}\]
if denominator is greater than 0 (\(p_Y(y) > 0\) or \(p_X(x) > 0\))







For continuous RVs:


\[f_{X|Y}(x|y) = \dfrac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}\] \[f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \dfrac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}\]
if denominator is greater than 0 (\(f_Y(y) > 0\) or \(f_X(x) > 0\))

title: Lesson 12: Independence and Conditioning
section: How do we represent independent RVs in a joint pmf/pdf?
text:
How do we represent independent RVs in a joint pmf/pdf?
What do we know about independence for events?
For events: If \(A \perp B\)
\[P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\] \[P(A|B) = P(A)\]




For discrete RVs: If \(X \perp Y\)


\[p_{X,Y}(x,y) = p_{X}(x)p_{Y}(y)\] \[F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_{X}(x)F_{Y}(y)\] \[p_{X|Y}(x|y) = p_{X}(x)\] \[p_{Y|X}(y|x) = p_{Y}(y)\]







For continuous RVs: If \(X \perp Y\)


\[f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{X}(x)f_{Y}(y)\] \[F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_{X}(x)F_{Y}(y)\] \[f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_{X}(x)\] \[f_{Y|X}(y|x) = f_{Y}(y)\]

title: Lesson 12: Independence and Conditioning
section: Remember: our probability rules must hold for these!
text:
Remember: our probability rules must hold for these!




For discrete RVs


For a valid joint pmf, we need:

\(0 \geq p_{X,Y}(x,y) \leq 1\) for all \(x, y\)
\(\sum \limits_{\{all\ x\}} \sum \limits_{\{all\ y\}} p_{X,Y}(x,y)=1\)

For a valid conditional pmf, we need:

\(0 \geq p_{X|Y}(x|y) \leq 1\) for all \(x, y\)
\(\sum \limits_{\{all\ x\}} p_{X|Y}(x|y)=1\)








For continuous RVs


For a valid joint pdf, we need:

\(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\geq 0\) for all \(x,y\)
\(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dxdy=1\)

For a valid conditional pdf, we need:

\(f_{X|Y}(x|y)\geq 0\) for all \(x\) and \(y\)
\(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx =1\)

title: Lesson 12: Independence and Conditioning
text:
Extra notes

If \(X_1, X_2, …, X_n\) are independent

\[p_{X_1, X_2, …, X_n}(x_1, x_2, …, x_n) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, …, X_n=x_n)=\prod\limits_{i=1}^np_{X_i}(x_i)\] \[f_{X_1, X_2, …, X_n}(x_1, x_2, …, x_n) = \prod\limits_{i=1}^nf_{X_i}(x_i)\] \[F_{X_1, X_2, …, X_n}(x_1, x_2, …, x_n) = P(X_1\leq x_1, X_2\leq x_2, …, X_n\leq x_n)=\prod\limits_{i=1}^nP(X_i \leq x_i) = \prod\limits_{i=1}^nF_{X_i}(x_i)\]

Don’t forget, you can manipulate the conditional density to get the joint: \[f_{X,Y}(x,y)= f_{X|Y}(x|y)f_Y(y)\]

title: Lesson 12: Independence and Conditioning
text:
Final statement on independence

If \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)= g(x)h(y)\), where \(g(x)\) and \(h(y)\) are pdf’s, then \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

The domain of the joint pdf needs to be independent as well!!


       

If \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)= G(x)H(y)\), where \(G(x)\) and \(H(y)\) are cdf’s, then \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

The domain of the joint CDF needs to be independent as well!!


       

Make sure that:

\(X\) domain does NOT depend on \(Y\)
\(Y\) domain does NOT depend on \(X\)
